different audiences, and how they should be viewed as a double feature. The trend was dubbed 
"Barbenheimer". In an interview with La Vanguardia, Oppenheimer star Cillian Murphy endorsed 
the phenomenon, saying, "My advice would be for people to go see both, on the same day. If they 
are good films, then that's cinema's gain."
In August 2023, it was announced that the film will be re-released in IMAX theaters on September 
22, 2023, for one week only, along with a new post-credit scene.
Home media
Barbie was released on digital download on September 12, 2023 and will be released on Ultra HD 
Blu-ray, Blu-ray, and DVD on January 2, 2024 by Warner Bros. Home Entertainment.
Box office
As of September 11, 2023, Barbie has grossed $620.7 million in the United States and Canada, and 
$783.5 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $1.404 billion.
It was described as a "record-breaking" box office success during its opening weekend, and set the 
record for any film that was not a sequel, remake, or superhero property. The film crossed the $1 
billion mark worldwide on August 6, 2023, making it the first film by a solo female director to do 
so. This was also the fastest Warner Bros. film to reach $1 billion, beating Harry Potter and the 
Deathly Hallows – Part 2 (2011). In late August, Barbie surpassed that same film again, becoming 
Warner Bros.'s highest-grossing film, not adjusted for inflation. By September 2, the film surpassed 
$1.365 billion at the global box office, overtaking The Super Mario Bros. Movie as the highest-
grossing film of the year. Additionally, it became the highest-grossing film by a solo female 
director, surpassing the previous records held by Wonder Woman (2017) and Hi, Mom (2021).
United States and Canada
In the United States and Canada, Barbie was released alongside Oppenheimer, and was originally 
projected to gross $90–125 million from 4,243 theaters in its opening weekend, with Warner Bros. 
predicting a $75 million debut. The week of their release, AMC Theatres announced that over 
40,000 AMC Stubs members had pre-booked tickets to both films on the same day. It earned $70.5 
million on its opening day, which included $22.3 million from Wednesday and Thursday night 
previews, both of which were the best of 2023. Barbie's opening weekend gross of $162 million 
marked the largest opening since Black Panther: Wakanda Forever ($181.3 million in November 
2022). It was also the biggest opening ever for a film helmed by a female director, besting Captain 
Marvel (2019), and surpassed Suicide Squad (2016) to have Robbie's highest opening weekend, as 
well as Blade Runner 2049 (2017) to have Gosling's largest opening weekend. It scored the third-
highest July opening weekend at the time, behind The Lion King (2019) and Harry Potter and the 
Deathly Hallows – Part 2. This also marked the third-highest opening weekend for a Warner Bros. 
film, after the latter film and Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016). Barbie also scored the 
biggest opening for a film based on a toy, surpassing Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen (2009). 
The Barbenheimer phenomenon was widely credited with boosting interest in the film, with a total 
of 79% of tickets sold over the weekend (52% for Barbie) being for the two films, a total of 18.5 
million people.
Following its opening weekend, Barbie surpassed The Dark Knight (2008) as the highest Monday 
gross ever for a Warner Bros. film, collecting a total of $26.1 million. In its second weekend, the 
film earned $92 million, dropping by 43%, which was the largest sophomore weekend ever for a 
Warner Bros. film and the seventh-largest ever. The film remained in first place with $53 million in 
its third weekend, and $33.7 million in its fourth weekend. On August 16, 2023, Barbie once again 
surpassed The Dark Knight; this time as the highest-grossing domestic release in Warner Bros.

Barbie (film)
Barbie is a 2023 American fantasy comedy film directed by Greta Gerwig from a screenplay she 
wrote with Noah Baumbach. Based on the eponymous fashion dolls by Mattel, it is the first live-
action Barbie film after numerous computer-animated films and specials. The film stars Margot 
Robbie as the titular character and Ryan Gosling as Ken, and follows the pair on a journey of self-
discovery following an existential crisis. It features a supporting cast that includes America Ferrera, 
Kate McKinnon, Issa Rae, Rhea Perlman, and Will Ferrell.
A live-action Barbie film was announced in September 2009 by Universal Pictures with Laurence 
Mark producing. Development began in April 2014, when Sony Pictures acquired the film rights. 
Following multiple writer and director changes and the casting of Amy Schumer and later Anne 
Hathaway as Barbie, the rights were transferred to Warner Bros. Pictures in October 2018. Robbie 
was cast in 2019, after Gal Gadot turned down the role due to scheduling conflicts, and Gerwig was 
announced as director and co-writer with Baumbach in 2020. The rest of the cast was announced in 
early 2022, with principal photography occurring primarily at Warner Bros. Studios, Leavesden, in 
England and at the Venice Beach Skatepark in Los Angeles from March to July of that year.
Barbie premiered at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on July 9, 2023, and was released in the 
United States on July 21, by Warner Bros. Pictures. Its simultaneous release with Universal's 
Oppenheimer led to the "Barbenheimer" cultural phenomenon, which encouraged audiences to see 
both films as a double feature. The film received critical acclaim and has grossed over $1.404 
billion, becoming the highest-grossing film of 2023 as well as the highest-grossing film by a solo 
female director, the highest-grossing film ever released by Warner Bros., and the 14th highest-
grossing film of all time.
Plot
Stereotypical Barbie ("Barbie") and fellow dolls reside in Barbieland; a matriarchal society with 
different variations of Barbies, Kens, and a group of discontinued models, who are treated like 
outcasts due to their unconventional traits. While the Kens spend their days playing at the beach, 
considering it as their profession, the Barbies hold prestigious jobs such as doctors, lawyers, and 
politicians. Beach Ken ("Ken") is only happy when he is with Barbie and seeks a closer 
relationship, but Barbie rebuffs him in favor of other activities and female friendships.
One evening at a dance party, Barbie is suddenly stricken with worries about mortality. Overnight, 
she develops bad breath, cellulite, and flat feet, disrupting her usual routines the next day. Weird 
Barbie, an outcast due to her disfigurement, tells her she must find the child playing with her in the 
real world to cure her afflictions. Ken stows away in her convertible to join her, to which Barbie 
reluctantly agrees.
Arriving at Venice Beach, Barbie punches a man for groping her, leading to her and Ken's brief 
arrest. Alarmed by their presence, Mattel's CEO orders their recapture. Barbie tracks down her 
owner, a tween girl named Sasha, who criticizes her for encouraging unrealistic beauty standards. 
Distraught, Barbie discovers that Gloria, a Mattel employee and Sasha's mother, inadvertently 
catalyzed her existential crisis after Gloria began playing with Sasha's old Barbie toys in a similar 
state. Mattel attempts to put Barbie in a toy box for remanufacturing, but she escapes with Gloria 
and Sasha's help and the three travel to Barbieland with Mattel executives in pursuit.
Meanwhile, Ken learns about the patriarchal system and feels respected for the first time. Returning
to Barbieland, he persuades the other Kens to take over, and the Barbies are indoctrinated into 
submissive roles, such as agreeable girlfriends, housewives, and maids. Barbie arrives and

(2002), was outraged with the decision as he had been a proponent of film theaters.[49] In January 
2021, media reports mentioned the possibility that Nolan's next film could be the first not to be 
financed or distributed by Warner Bros.[50] By mid-2021, the filmmaker had left Warner Bros. and 
was meeting with other studios to develop his new project.[2] Nolan had previously supported the 
studio's decision to give Wonder Woman 1984 (2020) a simultaneous release, stating that he 
perceived that situation to have been handled properly, but said he had been excluded from any 
discussions regarding the postponed release of Tenet.[51][52]
In September 2021, it was announced that Nolan would write and direct a biographical film set 
during World War II about Oppenheimer, with Cillian Murphy in negotiations to star.[53][54] Due 
to his strained relationship with Warner Bros., Nolan approached multiple studios for the project, 
including Sony Pictures, Universal Pictures, Paramount Pictures, and Apple Studios.[55][56] 
According to insiders, Paramount was ruled out early in the process in relation to the replacement of
CEO and chairman Jim Gianopulos with Brian Robbins, an advocate for increased streaming-
service releases.[56] Nolan had connections to Donna Langley, the chairman and chief content 
officer of the NBCUniversal studio group, who agreed with his stance in favor of traditional film 
exhibition in movie theaters. As such, Universal agreed to finance and distribute the film, with 
production set to begin in the first quarter of 2022.[57] The studio also agreed to Nolan's terms, 
which included a production budget of $100 million, an equal marketing budget, an exclusive 
theatrical window ranging from 90–120 days, 20% of the film's first-dollar gross, and a three-week 
period before and after the film's release in which Universal could not release another new film.

destroy the world.
After Germany surrenders, several scientists question the bomb's continued importance, even 
though the war in the Pacific is ongoing. The Trinity test is successfully conducted just before the 
Potsdam Conference. President Harry S. Truman orders the Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and 
Nagasaki, forcing Japan's surrender and thrusting Oppenheimer into the public eye as the "father of 
the atomic bomb". Haunted by the immense destruction and loss of life, Oppenheimer urges Truman
to restrict nuclear weapon development, which the president, calling Oppenheimer a "crybaby", 
disregards.
As an advisor to the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, Oppenheimer advocates against further 
nuclear research, especially the hydrogen bomb proposed by Teller. His stance becomes a point of 
contention amid the tense Cold War with the Soviet Union. AEC Chairman Lewis Strauss resents 
Oppenheimer for publicly dismissing his concerns regarding the export of radioisotopes and for 
recommending arms talks with the Soviet Union. He also believes Oppenheimer turned Einstein 
against him.
At a hearing intended to eliminate Oppenheimer's political influence, Oppenheimer is betrayed by 
Teller and other colleagues. Strauss exploits Oppenheimer's associations with communists such as 
Tatlock and Oppenheimer's brother, Frank. Despite Rabi and several other allies testifying in 
Oppenheimer's defense, Oppenheimer's security clearance is prematurely revoked, damaging his 
public image and neutralizing his policy influence. At Strauss's later Senate confirmation hearing to 
become Secretary of Commerce, Hill testifies about Strauss's personal motives in engineering 
Oppenheimer's downfall. The Senate votes against Strauss's nomination.
In 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson presents Oppenheimer with the Enrico Fermi Award as a 
gesture of political rehabilitation. It is revealed that Oppenheimer and Einstein's conversation was 
not about Strauss, but the far-reaching implications of nuclear weapons; Oppenheimer believes he 
personally started a chain reaction that will destroy the world.
Development
Following the 2005 publication of the biography American Prometheus by Bird and Sherwin, 
director Sam Mendes had been interested in adapting the book into a film. However, that project 
never materialized. Over the next 15 years, as the book was optioned by various filmmakers, the 
authors grew pessimistic about seeing their work adapted to the silver screen. In 2015, J. David 
Wargo optioned the book, then commissioned and rejected several scripts. During the COVID-19 
pandemic, Wargo flew to Hollywood to meet with actor James Woods, who set up a meeting with 
Charles Roven, a producer for various Christopher Nolan films, and in turn, Roven gave a copy of 
the book to Nolan. Both Wargo and Woods are executive producers of the film.[46]
Even before reading the book, Nolan had already long wanted to make a film about Oppenheimer.
[47] In 2019, towards the end of production on Nolan's science-fiction film Tenet (2020), star 
Robert Pattinson gave the director a book of Oppenheimer's speeches. According to Nolan, the 
speeches showed the physicist "wrestling with the implications ... of what's happened and what 
[he's] done". Nolan wanted to depict "what it would have been like to be Oppenheimer in those 
moments" in contrast to Tenet, which employs time travel to curb a potential weapon of mass 
destruction.[48][2]

releases in theaters and on HBO Max, citing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the film

Oppenheimer (film)
Oppenheimer is a 2023 biographical drama film written and directed by Christopher Nolan. Based 
on the 2005 biography American Prometheus by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin, the film 
chronicles the life of American theoretical physicist and polymath J. Robert Oppenheimer. The 
story predominantly focuses on Oppenheimer's early studies, his direction of the Manhattan Project 
during World War II, and his eventual fall from grace due to his 1954 security hearing; juxtaposed 
with this are events surrounding Oppenheimer's relationship with Lewis Strauss, a senior member 
of the United States Atomic Energy Commission who sees Oppenheimer as a rival. It stars Cillian 
Murphy as Oppenheimer and Robert Downey Jr. as Strauss, with the remaining ensemble 
supporting cast including Emily Blunt, Matt Damon, Florence Pugh, Josh Hartnett, Casey Affleck, 
Rami Malek and Kenneth Branagh.
The film was announced in September 2021 after Universal Pictures won a bidding war for Nolan's 
screenplay, following Nolan's conflict with longtime distributor Warner Bros. Pictures. Murphy was
the first cast member to be signed on, to portray Oppenheimer in October, with others in the main 
cast joining between November 2021 and April 2022. Pre-production was underway by January 
2022, with filming taking place from February to May. Oppenheimer was filmed in a combination 
of IMAX 65 mm and 65 mm large-format film, including, for the first time in history, sections in 
IMAX black-and-white film photography. It is Nolan's first film to receive R-rating since Insomnia 
(2002). Like his previous works, Nolan used extensive practical effects and minimal computer-
generated imagery.
Oppenheimer premiered at Le Grand Rex in Paris on July 11, 2023, and was theatrically released in 
the United States and United Kingdom on July 21, 2023, by Universal Pictures. Its simultaneous 
release with Warner Bros.' Barbie led to the "Barbenheimer" phenomenon on social media, which 
encouraged audiences to see both films as a double feature. The film has grossed over $412 million 
worldwide on a $100 million production budget and received critical acclaim, with particular praise 
for its cast, screenplay, and visuals.
Plot
The film is presented as a nonlinear narrative; this summary organizes the events in chronological 
order for the sake of clarity.
In 1926, 22-year-old doctoral student J. Robert Oppenheimer suffers from homesickness and 
anxiety while studying under experimental physicist Patrick Blackett at the Cavendish Laboratory 
in Cambridge. Upset with Blackett, Oppenheimer retaliates by leaving him a poisoned apple, then 
narrowly prevents visiting scientist Niels Bohr from eating it. Oppenheimer completes his PhD in 
physics at the University of Göttingen in Germany, where he meets theoretical physicist Werner 
Heisenberg. He returns to the United States, hoping to expand quantum physics research there, and 
begins teaching at the University of California, Berkeley and the California Institute of Technology. 
He meets his future wife, Katherine Puening, a biologist and ex-communist. He also has an 
intermittent affair with Jean Tatlock, a member of the Communist Party USA, until her suicide a 
few years later.
In 1942, U.S. Army General Leslie Groves recruits Oppenheimer to lead the Manhattan Project to 
develop an atomic bomb after Oppenheimer assures him he has no communist sympathies. 
Oppenheimer, who is Jewish, is particularly driven by the Nazis' potentially completing their 
nuclear weapons program that Heisenberg heads. Oppenheimer assembles a scientific team 
including Edward Teller and Isidor Isaac Rabi in Los Alamos, New Mexico to secretly create the 
bomb. Oppenheimer collaborates with scientists Enrico Fermi and David L. Hill, and he and Albert

ensuring that licensees continue to innovate and respond competitively to user needs.

wireless), subject to spectrum and other physical constraints.  Individual licenses for FBOs are 
awarded based on the merits of the applications, with license fees applicable.  The license 
duration provides the licensee with a degree of certainty in their operations, and IMDA

addition to the Broadcasting Act.   It entered into force on February 1, 2023.  The law requires 
social media platforms, but not private messaging communications, to implement measures to 
limit users’ exposure to online content the government deems to be harmful to the country.  
The law allows the government to designate platforms with significant reach and impact as

Pay-Television 
Mediacorp TV is the only free-to-air TV broadcaster and is 100 percent owned by the 
government via Temasek Holdings.  Mediacorp reported that its free-to-air channels are viewed 
weekly by 99 percent of residents at least once a month.  Local pay-TV providers are StarHub 
and Singtel, which are both partially owned by Temasek or its subsidiaries.  Local free-to-air 
radio broadcasters are Mediacorp Radio Singapore ( owned by Temasek Holdings), SPH Radio 
(owned by SPH Media Trust), and So Drama! Entertainment (owned by the Ministry of 
Defense).  BBC World Services is the only foreign free-to-air radio broadcaster in Singapore.

To rectify the high degree of content fragmentation in the Singaporean pay-TV market and shift 
the focus of competition from an exclusivity-centric strategy to other aspects, such as service 
differentiation and competitive packaging, the IMDA implemented cross-carriage measures in 
2011.  These measures required pay TV companies designated by IMDA to be Receiving 
Qualified Licensees (RQL) – currently Singtel and StarHub – to cross-carry content subject to

Banking and Finance 
Singapore is the leading financial services hub for Asia, excluding China/Hong Kong. 
Approximately 150 foreign banks operate in Singapore, alongside six local banks. Additionally, 
Singapore is home to a vast number of non-bank financial institutions, both domestic and 
foreign, including firms in: 
• financial advisory, 
• asset management, 
• insurance, and 
• capital markets. 
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) oversees all banking operations in the country per 
the Banking Act.  There are distinctions between foreign and local banks based on their 
licensing, which include: 
• full service, 
• wholesale, and 
• offshore banks.

As of April 2025, Singapore has 3 0 foreign banks with full-service licenses and 97 wholesale 
banks, as well as 21 merchant banks engaged in corporate finance and investment services.  It is 
important to note that offshore and wholesale banks are prohibited from participating in 
Singapore dollar retail banking.  Only full banks and “Qualifying Full Banks” (QFBs) can conduct 
retail banking for Singapore dollars, but they face limitations on their    number of business 
locations, automated teller machines (ATMs), and ATM networks.  As of April 2025, there are 
10 banks operating QFB licenses.

• cyberbullying, 
• terrorism,

Credit card holders from U.S. banks incorporated in Singapore cannot access their accounts 
through the local ATM networks.  They are also unable to access their accounts for cash 
withdrawals, transfers, or bill payments at ATMs operated by banks other than those operated 
by their own bank or at foreign banks’ shared ATM network.  Nevertheless, full-service foreign 
banks have made significant inroads in other retail banking areas, with substantial market share 
in products like credit cards and personal and housing loans.

(DPTs).  As of April 2025, Singapore has 33 Digital Payment Token Service providers.  Stablecoin 
adoption picked up steam in 2024 due to regulatory clarity provided by MAS when it finalized 
the stablecoin regulatory framework in late 2023.  In July 2024, Paxos became the first

In April 2023 the United States and Singapore announced the start of their joint Feasibility 
Study on Regional Energy Connectivity led by the U.S. Department of Energy.  The initial 
findings from the first phase of the joint study were announced in October 2023.  The second 
phase of the study is focused on evaluating the legal, technical, and governance frameworks as 
well as financing arrangements needed to facilitate regional energy connectivity and deepening 
the analysis of grid impacts. 
Currently, natural gas accounts for 95% of the country’s electricity generation and will continue 
to do so for the next decade as emphasized by Singapore in recent energy statements.  Natural

gas is currently piped in from neighboring countries, and LNG is shipped to Singapore from 
further afield.  Singapore wants to be an LNG bunkering hub and is developing plans for a 
second LNG terminal to complement its first terminal, which has been in operation for more 
than a decade.  The second facility will be a floating terminal, which is  currently under 
construction.  A new state-owned company, Gasco, has been set up to source and purchase 
LNG for Singapore.  The new company will help Singapore diversify its gas purchases and secure 
longer-term supplies, presenting opportunities for U.S. exporters.

MPRs have to be registered with the Energy Market Company (EMC) to purchase electricity 
from the National Electricity Market of Singapore (NEMS) to sell to contestable consumers.  
NMPRs need not register with EMC to participate in the NEMS since they will purchase 
electricity indirectly from the NEMS through the Market Support Services Licensee (MSSL).   In 
2021, a number of the electricity retailers withdrew from selling electricity due to high natural 
gas prices globally, resulting in unfavorable market conditions.  As of April 2024, there were 
nine retailers remaining in the market for residential consumers and 14 retailers for businesses,

Requirements for CII owners include: 
• a mandatory incident reporting regime, 
• regular audits and risk assessments, and 
• participation in national cyber security stress tests. 
In addition, the Act will establish a regulatory regime for cyber security service providers and 
required licensing for penetration testing and managed security operations center monitoring 
services. 
The Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill, introduced in Singapore’s Parliament on April 3, 2024, 
expands the Cyber Security Agency’s (CSA) oversight of organizations regulated by law.  The

agency.  CII owners will be allowed to use cloud infrastructure if the benefits outweigh the risks;

Cybersecurity 
As Singapore leverages technology to enhance the lives and livelihoods of its residents, it is 
seeking to ensure its initiatives are grounded in a robust cybersecurity framework.  Since 2015, 
the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) has sought to safeguard the nation’s cyberspace 
by raising cybersecurity awareness and building national resilience against cyber threats.  The 
Cybersecurity Act, which entered into force in August 2018, establishes a comprehensive 
regulatory framework for cybersecurity.  The Act provides the Commissioner of Cyber 
Security with powers to investigate, prevent, and assess the potential impact of cyber security

All accounting entities that provide public accountancy services must be approved under the 
Accountants Act and their supply of public accountancy services in Singapore must be under the 
control and management of partners or directors who are public accountants ordinarily 
resident in Singapore.  In addition, if the accounting entity firm has two partners or directors, at 
least one of them must be a public accountant.  If the business entity has more than two 
accounting partners or directors, two-thirds of the partners or directors must be public 
accountants.

Outward Investment 
Singapore places no restrictions on domestic investors investing abroad.  The government 
promotes outward investment through Enterprise Singapore, a statutory board under the 
Ministry of Trade and Industry.    It provides market information, business contacts, and financial 
assistance and grants for internationalizing companies.  While it has a global reach and runs 
overseas centers in major cities across the world, a large share of its overseas centers is located 
in major trading and investment partners and regional markets like: 
• China, 
• India, 
• the United States, and 
• ASEAN.

Section 2. Investment and Taxation Treaties 
Singapore has 44 bilateral investment treaties (BIT) currently in force.  These agreements 
mutually protect nationals or companies of either economy against non-commercial risks of 
expropriation and nationalization. 
Singapore has in force 14 bilateral, 13 regional free trade agreements (FTA), and four digital 
economy agreements.  In May 2025, Singapore and the EU signed the European Union-
Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, building on the Digital Trade Principles laid out in the EU-
Singapore Digital Partnership that was signed in 2023.   It signed a non-binding green economy 
agreement with Australia in 2022.  Singapore has signed free trade or economic cooperation

Singapore’s judicial system and courts serve as the oversight mechanism in respect of executive 
action (such as the enforcement of regulatory offences) and dispense justice based on law.  The 
Supreme Court, which is made up of the Court of Appeal and the High Court, hears both civil 
and criminal matters.  The chief justice heads the judiciary.  The President appoints the chief 
justice, the judges of appeal and the judges of the High Court if she, acting at her discretion, 
concurs with the advice of the Prime Minister.

ASEAN is working towards the 2025 ASEAN Economic Community Blueprint aimed at achieving 
a single market and production base, with a free flow of goods, services, and investment within 
the region.  While ASEAN is working towards regulatory harmonization, there are no regional 
regulatory systems in place; instead, ASEAN agreements and regulations are enacted through 
each ASEAN Member State’s domestic regulatory system.

courts of law.  The current judicial process is procedurally competent, fair, and reliable.   In the 
2024 Rule of Law Index by the World Justice Project, it is ranked 16th in the world overall, 
second on order and security, third on regulatory enforcement, third in absence of corruption, 
eighth on civil justice, seventh on criminal justice, 28th on constraints on government powers,

Dispute Settlement 
ICSID Convention and New York Convention 
Singapore is party to the Convention on the Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID 
Convention) and the convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitration 
Awards (1958 New York Convention).   Singapore passed an Arbitration (International 
Investment Disputes) Act to implement the ICSID Convention in 1968.  Singapore acceded to 
the 1958 New York Convention in August 1986 and gives effect to it via the International 
Arbitration Act (IAA).  The 1958 New York Convention is annexed to the IAA as the Second 
Schedule.  Singapore is bound to recognize awards made in any other country that is a signatory 
to the 1958 New York Convention.

Expropriation and Compensation 
Singapore has not expropriated foreign-owned property and has no laws that force foreign 
investors to transfer ownership to local interests.  Singapore has signed investment promotion 
and protection agreements with a wide range of countries.  These agreements mutually protect 
nationals or companies of either country against certain non-commercial risks, such as 
expropriation and nationalization and remain in effect unless otherwise terminated.  The 
USSFTA contains strong investor protection provisions relating to expropriation of private 
property and the need to follow due process; provisions are in place for an owner to receive 
compensation based on fair market value.  No disputes are pending.

The Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act passed in 2018 and entered into force in July 
2020.  It updates the insolvency legislation and introduces a significant number of new 
provisions, particularly with respect to corporate insolvency.   It mandates licensing,

Singapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable 
Investment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in 
Singapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s 
Global Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, 
expansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as 
implementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is 
applicable to both domestic and foreign investors.

Foreign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation 
Singapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be 
used for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore 
for subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local 
firms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. 
Performance and Data Localization Requirements

decrease in estimated software piracy from 35 percent in 2009 to 27 percent at present, the 
index noted that piracy levels remain high for a developed, high-income economy.  Lack of 
transparency and data on customs seizures of IP-infringing goods is also noted as a key area of 
weakness. 
Singapore does not publicly report the statistics on seizures of counterfeit goods and does not 
rate highly on enforcement of physical counterfeit goods, online sales of counterfeit goods, or 
digital online piracy, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s International IP Index.

The availability of covered bond legislation under MAS Notice 648 has provided an incentive for 
Singapore financial institutions to issue covered bonds.  Under Notice 648, only a bank 
incorporated in Singapore may issue covered bonds.  The three main Singapore banks have 
covered bond programs offer issues to private investors: 
• DBS, 
• OCBC, and 
• UOB. 
In 2020, MAS increased the asset encumbrance limit of a locally incorporated bank’s total 
assets from 4 percent to 10 percent.  The banking industry has made suggestions to allow the 
use of covered bonds in repossession transactions with the central bank.

Intellectual Property Rights 
Singapore maintains one of the strongest intellectual property rights regimes in Asia.  The 
current Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization, Daren Tang, was 
formerly the chief executive of the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore.    Singapore is the 
global hub for patent filing activity and innovation.

Section 6. Financial Sector 
Capital Markets and Portfolio Investment 
The government takes a favorable stance towards foreign portfolio investment and fixed asset 
investments.  While it welcomes capital market investments, the government has introduced 
macro-prudential policies aimed at reducing foreign speculative inflows in the real estate sector 
since 2009.  The government promotes Singapore’s position as an asset and wealth 
management center.  Singapore’s assets   under management increased by 10 percent in 2023 to 
$4.1 trillion, according to MAS’s Singapore Asset Management Survey 2023. 
The government facilitates the free flow of financial resources into product and factor markets,

can access credit, U.S. dollars, SGD, and other foreign currencies on the local market.  The 
private sector has access to a variety of credit instruments through banks operating in 
Singapore.  The government respects IMF Article VIII by refraining from restrictions on 
payments and transfers for current international transactions.

There are no restrictions on foreign ownership of industrial and commercial real estate.  
Foreigners who purchase homes in Singapore are required to pay an additional effective 60 
percent tax on top of standard buyer’s taxes.   However, U.S. citizens are accorded national 
treatment under the FTA, meaning only second and subsequent purchases of residential 
property will be subject to 20 and 30 percent additional duties, equivalent to Singaporean 
citizens.

profile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment,

In January 2020, the Payment Services Bill went into effect, which will require all 
cryptocurrency service providers to be licensed with the intent to provide more user 
protection.  Smaller payment firms will receive a different classification from larger institutions

Foreign Exchange and Remittances 
Foreign Exchange 
The USSFTA commits Singapore to the free transfer of capital, unimpeded by regulatory 
restrictions.  Singapore places no restrictions on reinvestment or repatriation of earnings and 
capital, and maintains no significant restrictions on remittances, foreign exchange transactions 
and capital movements.

Singapore was an early mover in creating a domestic fast payments system and has been a 
regional leader in promoting cross-border payments by establishing bilateral linkages for retail 
payments with five neighboring jurisdictions.  MAS is currently collaborating with other ASEAN 
central banks on creating what would be the region’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital 
retail payments hub (dubbed Project Nexus), with the aim of making it operational in the next 
few years.

Singapore’s banking system is sound and well regulated by MAS, and the country serves as a 
financial hub for the region.  Banks have a very high domestic penetration rate, and according 
to MAS in 2020, over 98 percent of adult Singapore residents held a financial account.  Local 
Singapore banks continued to see net profits increase in 2024, even as funding and operating 
costs rose.  Banks are statutorily prohibited from engaging in non-financial business.   Banks can 
hold 10 percent or less in non-financial companies as an “equity portfolio investment.”  The 
non-performing loans ratio (NPL ratio) of Singapore’s banking system remained below 2 
percent as of December 31, 2024, with the NPL ratio for DBS at 1.1 percent, UOB at 1.5 percent, 
and OCBC at 0.9 percent.

restricting the ability of some companies to hire foreign workers, including spouses of 
employment pass holders.  The government further regulates the inflow of and dependence on 
foreign workers through the Foreign Worker Levy (FWL) and the Dependency Ratio Ceiling 
(DRC).  The DRC is the maximum permitted ratio of foreign workers to the total workforce that 
a company can hire and serves as a quota on the hiring of foreign workers.  The DRC varies

Section 10. Labor Policies and Practices 
As of December 2024, Singapore’s labor market totaled 4.02 million workers; this includes 
about 1.58 million foreigners, of whom about 76 percent are basic skilled or semi-skilled 
workers (non-S Pass and Employment Pass holders).    The overall unemployment rate for the full 
year of 2024 was 2.0 percent.  Local labor laws allow for relatively free hiring and firing 
practices.  Either party can terminate employment by giving the other party the required 
notice.  The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) must approve employment of foreigners. 
Work Passes and Regulations 
All foreigners must have a valid work pass before they can start work in Singapore. From 
January 1, 2025, onwards, there are revised qualifying salaries for the most widely issued work

Singapore’s Parliament passed in September 2024 the Platform Workers Bill, which took effect 
on January 1, 2025, marking a significant shift in labor protections for gig economy workers 
such as ride-hailing drivers and food delivery personnel.  The legislation introduces a new 
worker category, distinct from traditional employees and the self-employed, acknowledging the 
unique nature of platform work.  Key provisions include mandatory Central Provident Fund 
(CPF) contributions from both platform operators and workers, phased in over five years to 
align with those of formal employees, enhancing retirement and housing adequacy.  
Additionally, platform workers are now entitled to work injury compensation comparable to

that of employees, with clear guidelines on liability when injuries occur during tasks involving 
multiple platforms.  The Act also establishes a legal framework for collective representation, 
allowing platform workers to engage in formal discussions on employment matters.  These 
measures aim to balance the flexibility inherent in gig work with essential protections, 
reflecting Singapore's commitment to adapting its labor laws to the evolving digital economy.

collective bargaining agreement before it is deemed in effect and can deny certification on 
public interest grounds. 
Dispute Management 
Most labor disagreements are resolved through conciliation and mediation by MOM.  Since 
April 2017, the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) under MOM provides 
advisory and mediation services, including mediation for salary and employment disputes.

Employment Claims Act (2016).  To bring a claim before the ECT, parties must first register their 
claims at the TADM for mediation.  Mediation at TADM is compulsory.  Only disputes which 
remain unresolved after mediation at TADM may be referred to the ECT.

consult with unions on both problems, and the Taskforce for Responsible Retrenchment and

on coverage of collective bargaining agreements is not publicly available.  The Industrial

Section 9. Political and Security Environment 
Singapore’s political environment is stable, and there is no recent history of incidents involving 
politically motivated damage to foreign investments in Singapore.  The ruling People’s Action 
Party (PAP) has dominated Singapore’s parliamentary government since 1959 and currently 
controls 87 of the 97 parliamentary seats.  The main opposition Workers’ Party   (WP), which 
currently holds 10 parliamentary seats and two non-constituency member of parliament seats, 
does not usually espouse views that are radically different from mainstream public opinion.

referred to the IAC.   The IAC has two panels:

Human Trafficking Act (PHTA) criminalizes human trafficking and empowers law enforcement to

of Home Affairs are responsible for combating labor trafficking and improving working

core provisions to managers and executives, increased monthly salary cap, the transfer of 
adjudication of wrongful dismissal claims from MOM to the ECT, and increased flexibility in 
compensating employees working during public holidays.  All workers, except for public 
servants, domestic workers and seafarers, are covered by the Employment Act and additional 
time-based provisions for more vulnerable employees.

Collective bargaining is a normal part of labor-management relations in all sectors.  Almost all 
unions are affiliated with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), the sole national 
federation of trade unions in Singapore, which has a close relationship with the ruling party PAP 
and the government.  The current NTUC secretary-general, Ng Chee Meng, won election to 
parliament in 2025 after losing his re-election bid in 2020.  He previously served as a minister in 
the Prime Minister’s Office.  As of April 2025, NTUC membership has surpassed 1.4 million.

Executive Summary 
Singapore maintains   an open, heavily trade-dependent economy that plays a critical role in the 
global supply chain.  It supports predominantly open investment policies and a robust free 
market economy while actively managing and sustaining Singapore’s economic development.  
U.S. companies regularly cite the following as attractive investment climate features: 
• transparency, 
• business-friendly laws, 
• tax structure, 
• customs facilitation, 
• intellectual property protection, and 
• well-developed infrastructure.

Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.     "pageContent": "Page 43 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \n• Berne Convention, \n• Patent Cooperation Treaty, \n• Madrid Protocol, and \n• Budapest Treaty. \nThe WIPO Secretariat opened a regional office in Singapore in 2005.  Amendments to the \nTrademark Act, which were passed in January 2007, fulfilled Singapore’s obligations in WIPO’s \nrevised Singapore Treaty on the Law of Trademarks. \nSingapore ranked 13th out of 55 countries in the 2025   U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s \nInternational Intellectual Property (IP) Index.  The index noted that Singapore’s key strengths \ninclude an advanced national IP framework and active efforts to accelerate patent prosecution.  \nThe index also lauded Singapore as a global leader in online copyright enforcement.  Despite a \ndecrease in estimated software piracy from 35 percent in 2009 to 27 percent at present, the \nindex noted that piracy levels remain high for a developed, high-income economy.  Lack of \ntransparency and data on customs seizures of IP-infringing goods is also noted as a key area of \nweakness. \nSingapore does not publicly report the statistics on seizures of counterfeit goods and does not \nrate highly on enforcement of physical counterfeit goods, online sales of counterfeit goods, or \ndigital online piracy, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s International IP Index.  \nSingapore is not listed in USTR’s 2025   Special 301 Report.  Shopee, a Singapore-headquartered \ne-  commerce company, has been named in USTR’s Review of Notorious Markets since 2021but \nthe 2024 review noted the company has made significant investments in expanding and \nstrengthening its anti-counterfeiting programs.  On the trade of counterfeit and pirated goods, \nstakeholders also continue to report dissatisfaction with border enforcement in Singapore, \nincluding concerns about the lack of coordination between Singapore’s Customs authorities and \nthe Singapore Police Force’s IP Rights Branch, although the latter has confirmed its intention to \nmore proactively enforce IP rights cases going forward. \nFor additional information about national laws and points of contact at local IP offices, see \nWIPO’s country profiles.     "pageContent": "Page 54 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nSection 9. Political and Security Environment \nSingapore’s political environment is stable, and there is no recent history of incidents involving \npolitically motivated damage to foreign investments in Singapore.  The ruling People’s Action \nParty (PAP) has dominated Singapore’s parliamentary government since 1959 and currently \ncontrols 87 of the 97 parliamentary seats.  The main opposition Workers’ Party   (WP), which \ncurrently holds 10 parliamentary seats and two non-constituency member of parliament seats, \ndoes not usually espouse views that are radically different from mainstream public opinion. \nSection 10. Labor Policies and Practices \nAs of December 2024, Singapore’s labor market totaled 4.02 million workers; this includes \nabout 1.58 million foreigners, of whom about 76 percent are basic skilled or semi-skilled \nworkers (non-S Pass and Employment Pass holders).    The overall unemployment rate for the full \nyear of 2024 was 2.0 percent.  Local labor laws allow for relatively free hiring and firing \npractices.  Either party can terminate employment by giving the other party the required \nnotice.  The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) must approve employment of foreigners. \nWork Passes and Regulations \nAll foreigners must have a valid work pass before they can start work in Singapore. From \nJanuary 1, 2025, onwards, there are revised qualifying salaries for the most widely issued work \npasses, namely the: \n• Employment Pass (EP), for professionals, managers, and executives earning at least \n$4,144   a month, or $4,588 for those in the financial services sector; \n• S Pass,  for mid-level skilled staff earning at least $2,442 a month, or $2,812 for those in \nthe financial services sector; and \n• Work Permits,  for semi-skilled workers such as migrant workers and migrant domestic \nworkers.     "pageContent": "Page 55 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nWorkers need to have a job with minimum fixed monthly salaries and acceptable qualifications \nto be eligible for the EP and S Pass.  MOM has increased minimum salaries multiple times, \nrestricting the ability of some companies to hire foreign workers, including spouses of \nemployment pass holders.  The government further regulates the inflow of and dependence on \nforeign workers through the Foreign Worker Levy (FWL) and the Dependency Ratio Ceiling \n(DRC).  The DRC is the maximum permitted ratio of foreign workers to the total workforce that \na company can hire and serves as a quota on the hiring of foreign workers.  The DRC varies \nacross sectors.  Employers of S Pass and Work Permit holders are required to pay a monthly \nFWL for each foreign worker to the government.  The FWL varies according to the skills, \nqualifications, and experience of their employees.  The FWL is set on a sector-by-sector basis \nand is subject to annual revisions.  FWLs have been progressively increased for most sectors \nsince 2012.  Refer to Ministry of Manpower (MOM) for more information on quota and levy \nrates. \nSingapore recorded its highest number of foreign workers again in 2024 (1,576,000),  resulting \nin an increase in Singapore’s population to a record high of 6.04 million as of June 2024.  The \nbulk of the increase came from non-residents, including work permit holders and migrant \ndomestic workers, which grew 5 percent from 1.77 million in June 2023 to 1.86 million in June \n2024.  Singapore faces   significant demographic headwinds from an aging population and low \nbirth rates, alongside restrictions on foreign workers.   Singapore’s local workforce growth is \nslowing as well, further increasing the need for foreign workers. \nTo address concerns over an aging and shrinking workforce, MOM has expanded its training \nand grant programs to support productivity.  An example of an existing program is SkillsFuture, \na government initiative managed by SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG), a statutory board under the \nMinistry of Education, designed to provide all Singaporeans with enhanced opportunities and \nskills-capacity building.  SSG also administers the Singapore Workforce Skills Qualifications, a \nnational credential system that trains, develops, assesses, and certifies skills and competencies \nfor the workforce.  The government also launched a new “Jobs-Skills Integrators” program in \nBudget 2023 that would serve as an intermediary to strengthen the training and placement \necosystem by engaging enterprises and training providers to understand skills gaps and update \nexisting training programs.     "pageContent": "Page 39 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nSection 4. Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.  Singapore has no forced localization policy requiring domestic content in \ngoods or technology.  The government does not require investors to purchase from local ",

    "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA.  Since 2006, U.S.-licensed full-service \nbanks that are also QFBs have been able to operate at an unlimited number of locations \n(branches or off-premises ATMs) versus 25 for non-U.S. full service foreign banks with QFB \nstatus. \nUnder the OECD CRS, which has been in effect since January 2017, Singapore-based financial \ninstitutions – depository institutions such as banks, specified insurance companies, investment \nentities, and custodial institutions – are required to: \n• establish the tax residency status of all their account holders; \n• collect and retain CRS information for all non-Singapore tax residents in the case of new \naccounts; and \n• report to tax authorities the financial account information of account holders who are \ntax residents of jurisdictions with which Singapore has a Competent Authority \nAgreement to exchange the information. \nU.S. financial regulations do not restrict foreign banks’ ability to hold accounts for U.S. citizens.  \nU.S. citizens are encouraged to alert the nearest U.S. Embassy of any practices they encounter \nwith regard to the provision of financial services. \nMAS has worked to position Singapore as a regional and global leader in financial technology \ninnovation.  Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.  This reflected the global trend in 2024, where uncertainty related to \nongoing macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical conflicts and tensions, and a number of high-\nprofile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment, \nparticularly on the mergers and acquisitions and private equity fronts.  To strengthen \nSingapore’s position as a global fintech hub, MAS has created a dedicated Fintech Office as a \none-stop virtual entity for all fintech-related matters to enable experimentation and promote \nan open-API (Application Programming Interfaces) in the financial industry.  According to \nKPMG’s Pulse of Fintech report, despite reduced funding levels globally, Singapore’s focus on \ninnovation and sustainability positions it as a leader in AI-driven solutions and blockchain ",

    "pageContent": "Page 2 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \n• machinery, and equipment \n• and services: \no financial, \no trade, \no and business. \nThe government actively promotes the country as a research and development (R&D) and \ninnovation center for businesses by offering tax incentives, research grants, and partnership \nopportunities with domestic research agencies.  U.S. foreign direct investment (FDI) stock in \nSingapore in 2023 totaled $424 billion, primarily in non-bank holding companies, \nmanufacturing, wholesale trade, and finance and insurance.  Singapore received more than \ndouble the U.S. FDI invested in any other Southeast Asian nation.  The investment outlook is \npositive due to Singapore’s proximity to Southeast Asia’s developing economies with their \npositive demographic trends.  Singapore remains a regional hub for thousands of multinational \ncompanies and continues to maintain its reputation as a world leader in dispute resolution, \nfinancing, and project facilitation for regional infrastructure development. \nSingapore is well-poised to attract future foreign investment in digital innovation, \npharmaceutical manufacturing, sustainable development, and cybersecurity.  Singapore is \ninvesting heavily in automation, artificial intelligence, integrated systems,  as well as \nsustainability, and seeks to establish itself as a regional hub for these technologies.  Singapore is \nalso a well-established hub for medical research and device manufacturing. \nSingapore’s Significant Investments Review Act came into force in March 2024.  The new Act \nempowers   the Ministry of Trade and Industry to designate entities as critical to national \nsecurity interests.  An Office of Significant Investments Review (OSIR) was established under \nMTI to administer and operationalize the Act.  Designated entities must seek the Trade and \nIndustry Minister’s approval for purchases or sales of controlling stakes in the entities and \nappointment of key officers if such changes exceed certain thresholds.  The new mechanism \ncomplements   and mirrors existing powers the authorities have over entities in sectors covered \nby prior legislation, such as in the banking and telecommunications sectors.     "pageContent": "Page 15 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \ninstitutions to explore and pilot new fintech applications, focusing on cross-border payments, \ndigital assets, tokenization, and AI adoption. \nRecognized as a pioneer in establishing a domestic fast payment system, Singapore is also a \nregional advocate for cross-border payments and is working on expanding bilateral links for \nretail payments.  MAS is collaborating with other ASEAN central banks to launch Project Nexus, \nthe world’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital retail payments hub, which is expected to \nbe operational in the coming years. \nWhile MAS does not currently perceive a strong use case for a retail central bank digital \ncurrency (CBDC), it is exploring the feasibility and utility of a wholesale CBDC, particularly for \ncross-border settlement purposes. \nLegal Services \nThe Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) under the Ministry of Law oversees the \nregulation, licensing, and compliance of all law practice entities and the registration of foreign \nlawyers in Singapore.   Foreign law firms with a licensed Foreign Law Practice (FLP) may offer the \nfull range of legal services in foreign law and international law but cannot practice Singapore \nlaw except in the context of international commercial arbitration.  U.S. and foreign attorneys \nare allowed to represent parties in arbitration without the need for a Singaporean attorney to \nbe present.  To offer Singapore law services, FLPs require either a Qualifying Foreign Law \nPractice (QFLP) license, a Joint Law Venture (JLV) with a Singapore Law Practice (SLP), or a \nFormal Law Alliance (FLA) with a SLP.  The vast majority of Singapore’s foreign law firms operate \nFLPs. \nThe QFLP licenses allow foreign law firms to practice in permitted areas of Singapore law, which \nexcludes constitutional and administrative law, conveyancing, criminal law, family law, \nsuccession law, and trust law.  Decisions on QFLP licenses renewal take into consideration the \nfirms’ quantitative and qualitative performance, such as the value of work that the Singapore \noffice will generate, the extent to which the Singapore office will function as the firm’s \nheadquarter for the region, the firm’s contributions to Singapore, and the firm’s proposal for ",

    "pageContent": "Page 32 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \non relevant websites.  As noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, some U.S. \ncompanies, in particular in the telecommunications and media sectors, are concerned about \nthe government's lack of transparency in its regulatory and rule-making process.   However, \nmany U.S. firms report they have opportunities to weigh in on pending legislation that affects \ntheir industries.   These mechanisms also apply to investment laws and regulations. \nThe Parliament of Singapore publishes a database of all bills introduced, read, and passed in \nparliament, in chronological order as of 2006.  The contents are the actual draft texts of the \nproposed legislation or legislative amendments.  All statutes are also publicly available in the \nSingapore Statutes Online website.  However, there is no centralized online location where key \nregulatory actions are published.   Regulatory actions are published separately on websites of \nStatutory Boards. \nEnforcement of regulatory offences is governed by both acts of parliament and subsidiary \nlegislation.  Enforcement powers of government statutory bodies are typically enshrined in the \nact of parliament constituting that statutory body.  There is accountability to parliament for \nenforcement action through question time, where members of parliament may raise questions \nwith the ministers on their respective ministries’ responsibilities. \nSingapore’s judicial system and courts serve as the oversight mechanism in respect of executive \naction (such as the enforcement of regulatory offences) and dispense justice based on law.  The \nSupreme Court, which is made up of the Court of Appeal and the High Court, hears both civil \nand criminal matters.  The chief justice heads the judiciary.  The President appoints the chief \njustice, the judges of appeal and the judges of the High Court if she, acting at her discretion, \nconcurs with the advice of the Prime Minister. \nNo systemic regulatory reforms or enforcement reforms relevant to foreign investors were \nannounced in recent years.  The MAS focuses enforcement efforts on timely disclosure of \ncorporate information, business conduct of financial advisors, compliance with anti-money \nlaundering or combatting the financing of terrorism requirements, deterring stock market \nabuse, and insider trading.  MAS has published enforcement reports detailing enforcement \nmeasures and publishes recent enforcement actions on its website annually since 2019. ",

The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system. It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions.     "pageContent": "Page 32 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \non relevant websites.  As noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, some U.S. \ncompanies, in particular in the telecommunications and media sectors, are concerned about \nthe government's lack of transparency in its regulatory and rule-making process.   However, \nmany U.S. firms report they have opportunities to weigh in on pending legislation that affects \ntheir industries.   These mechanisms also apply to investment laws and regulations. \nThe Parliament of Singapore publishes a database of all bills introduced, read, and passed in \nparliament, in chronological order as of 2006.  The contents are the actual draft texts of the \nproposed legislation or legislative amendments.  All statutes are also publicly available in the \nSingapore Statutes Online website.  However, there is no centralized online location where key \nregulatory actions are published.   Regulatory actions are published separately on websites of \nStatutory Boards. \nEnforcement of regulatory offences is governed by both acts of parliament and subsidiary \nlegislation.  Enforcement powers of government statutory bodies are typically enshrined in the \nact of parliament constituting that statutory body.  There is accountability to parliament for \nenforcement action through question time, where members of parliament may raise questions \nwith the ministers on their respective ministries’ responsibilities. \nSingapore’s judicial system and courts serve as the oversight mechanism in respect of executive \naction (such as the enforcement of regulatory offences) and dispense justice based on law.  The \nSupreme Court, which is made up of the Court of Appeal and the High Court, hears both civil \nand criminal matters.  The chief justice heads the judiciary.  The President appoints the chief \njustice, the judges of appeal and the judges of the High Court if she, acting at her discretion, \nconcurs with the advice of the Prime Minister. \nNo systemic regulatory reforms or enforcement reforms relevant to foreign investors were \nannounced in recent years.  The MAS focuses enforcement efforts on timely disclosure of \ncorporate information, business conduct of financial advisors, compliance with anti-money \nlaundering or combatting the financing of terrorism requirements, deterring stock market \nabuse, and insider trading.  MAS has published enforcement reports detailing enforcement \nmeasures and publishes recent enforcement actions on its website annually since 2019. ",

    "pageContent": "Page 30 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \norganizations that have been given autonomy to perform an operational function by legal \nstatutes passed as acts of parliament, and report to a specific ministry.  Local laws give \nregulatory bodies wide discretion to modify regulations and impose new conditions, but in \npractice agencies use this positively to adapt incentives or other services on a case-by-case \nbasis to meet the needs of foreign as well as domestic companies.  Acts of parliament also \nconfer certain powers on a minister or other similar persons or authorities to make rules or \nregulations in order to put the act into practice; these rules are known as subsidiary legislation.  \nNational-level regulations are the most relevant for foreign businesses.  Singapore has no local \nor state regulatory layers. \nBefore a ministry instructs the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) to draft a new bill or make \nan amendment to a bill, the ministry has to seek in-principle approval from the cabinet for the \nproposed bill.  The AGC legislation division advises and helps vet or draft bills in conjunction \nwith policymakers from relevant ministries.   Public and private consultations are often \nrequested for proposed draft legislative amendments.  Thereafter, the cabinet’s approval is \nrequired before the bill can be introduced in parliament.   All bills passed by parliament (with \nsome exceptions) must be forwarded to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights for \nscrutiny, and thereafter presented to the President for assent.  Only after the President has \nassented to the bill does it become law. \nWhile ministries or regulatory agencies do conduct internal impact assessments of proposed \nreg\nulations, there are no criteria used for determining which proposed regulations are \nsubjected to an impact assessment, and there are no specific regulatory impact assessment \nguidelines.  There is no independent agency tasked with reviewing and monitoring regulatory \nimpact assessments and distributing findings to the public.  The Ministry of Finance publishes a \nbiennial Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, focusing on broad outcomes and indicators \nrather than policy evaluation. For a U.S. fintech company looking to establish operations in Singapore, key regulatory requirements include obtaining the appropriate licenses from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), adhering to regulatory frameworks specific to fintech operations, and ensuring compliance with local tax and employment regulations.

**Key Facts & Regulations**  
- A fintech company must secure the necessary licenses from the MAS, which may include a license to operate as a payment service provider or a financial adviser, depending on their specific business model (Section: Regulatory requirements for fintech firms, p.2).
- The Payment Services Act (PSA) introduced a regulatory framework for various payment services, and firms engaged in payment services will need to comply with this act (Section: Licensing requirements for fintech firms, p.3).
- U.S. fintech companies must also understand their tax obligations, including corporate income tax rates and the applicability of tax treaties between the U.S. and Singapore (Section: Tax implications for U.S. companies, p.4).
- Employers must comply with local employment regulations, which include adhering to the Employment Act and ensuring proper work passes for foreign employees (Section: Employment regulations for hiring, p.5).

**Recommendations**  
- Engage with a local legal or consulting firm to navigate the licensing process and ensure compliance with the MAS regulations specific to fintech.
- Conduct a thorough analysis of tax implications and potential incentives for foreign fintech companies operating in Singapore.
- Familiarize yourself with local employment laws and consider workforce local hiring strategies to comply with regulations regarding foreign workers.

    "pageContent": "Page 32 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \non relevant websites.  As noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, some U.S. \ncompanies, in particular in the telecommunications and media sectors, are concerned about \nthe government's lack of transparency in its regulatory and rule-making process.   However, \nmany U.S. firms report they have opportunities to weigh in on pending legislation that affects \ntheir industries.   These mechanisms also apply to investment laws and regulations. \nThe Parliament of Singapore publishes a database of all bills introduced, read, and passed in \nparliament, in chronological order as of 2006.  The contents are the actual draft texts of the \nproposed legislation or legislative amendments.  All statutes are also publicly available in the \nSingapore Statutes Online website.  However, there is no centralized online location where key \nregulatory actions are published.   Regulatory actions are published separately on websites of \nStatutory Boards. \nEnforcement of regulatory offences is governed by both acts of parliament and subsidiary \nlegislation.  Enforcement powers of government statutory bodies are typically enshrined in the \nact of parliament constituting that statutory body.  There is accountability to parliament for \nenforcement action through question time, where members of parliament may raise questions \nwith the ministers on their respective ministries’ responsibilities. \nSingapore’s judicial system and courts serve as the oversight mechanism in respect of executive \naction (such as the enforcement of regulatory offences) and dispense justice based on law.  The \nSupreme Court, which is made up of the Court of Appeal and the High Court, hears both civil \nand criminal matters.  The chief justice heads the judiciary.  The President appoints the chief \njustice, the judges of appeal and the judges of the High Court if she, acting at her discretion, \nconcurs with the advice of the Prime Minister. \nNo systemic regulatory reforms or enforcement reforms relevant to foreign investors were \nannounced in recent years.  The MAS focuses enforcement efforts on timely disclosure of \ncorporate information, business conduct of financial advisors, compliance with anti-money \nlaundering or combatting the financing of terrorism requirements, deterring stock market \nabuse, and insider trading.  MAS has published enforcement reports detailing enforcement \nmeasures and publishes recent enforcement actions on its website annually since 2019. ",

Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore. The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.     "pageContent": "Page 30 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \norganizations that have been given autonomy to perform an operational function by legal \nstatutes passed as acts of parliament, and report to a specific ministry. Acts of parliament also \nconfer certain powers on a minister or other similar persons or authorities to make rules or \nregulations in order to put the act into practice; these rules are known as subsidiary legislation.  \nNational-level regulations are the most relevant for foreign businesses.  Singapore has no local \nor state regulatory layers. \nBefore a ministry instructs the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) to draft a new bill or make \nan amendment to a bill, the ministry has to seek in-principle approval from the cabinet for the \nproposed bill.  The AGC legislation division advises and helps vet or draft bills in conjunction \nwith policymakers from relevant ministries.   Public and private consultations are often \nrequested for proposed draft legislative amendments.  Thereafter, the cabinet’s approval is \nrequired before the bill can be introduced in parliament.   All bills passed by parliament (with \nsome exceptions) must be forwarded to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights for \nscrutiny, and thereafter presented to the President for assent.  Only after the President has \nassented to the bill does it become law. \nWhile ministries or regulatory agencies do conduct internal impact assessments of proposed \nreg\nulations, there are no criteria used for determining which proposed regulations are \nsubjected to an impact assessment, and there are no specific regulatory impact assessment \nguidelines.  There is no independent agency tasked with reviewing and monitoring regulatory \nimpact assessments and distributing findings to the public.  The Ministry of Finance publishes a \nbiennial Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, focusing on broad outcomes and indicators \nrather than policy evaluation. MAS is collaborating with other ASEAN central banks to launch Project Nexus, \nthe world’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital retail payments hub, which is expected to \nbe operational in the coming years. \nWhile MAS does not currently perceive a strong use case for a retail central bank digital \ncurrency (CBDC), it is exploring the feasibility and utility of a wholesale CBDC, particularly for \ncross-border settlement purposes. \nLegal Services \nThe Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) under the Ministry of Law oversees the \nregulation, licensing, and compliance of all law practice entities and the registration of foreign \nlawyers in Singapore.   Foreign law firms with a licensed Foreign Law Practice (FLP) may offer the \nfull range of legal services in foreign law and international law but cannot practice Singapore \nlaw except in the context of international commercial arbitration.  U.S. and foreign attorneys \nare allowed to represent parties in arbitration without the need for a Singaporean attorney to \nbe present.  To offer Singapore law services, FLPs require either a Qualifying Foreign Law \nPractice (QFLP) license, a Joint Law Venture (JLV) with a Singapore Law Practice (SLP), or a \nFormal Law Alliance (FLA) with a SLP. RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore. Singapore received more than \ndouble the U.S. FDI invested in any other Southeast Asian nation. Singapore is \ninvesting heavily in automation, artificial intelligence, integrated systems,  as well as \nsustainability, and seeks to establish itself as a regional hub for these technologies.  Singapore is \nalso a well-established hub for medical research and device manufacturing. \nSingapore’s Significant Investments Review Act came into force in March 2024. Local laws give \nregulatory bodies wide discretion to modify regulations and impose new conditions, but in \npractice agencies use this positively to adapt incentives or other services on a case-by-case \nbasis to meet the needs of foreign as well as domestic companies.  Acts of parliament also \nconfer certain powers on a minister or other similar persons or authorities to make rules or \nregulations in order to put the act into practice; these rules are known as subsidiary legislation.  \nNational-level regulations are the most relevant for foreign businesses.  Singapore has no local \nor state regulatory layers. \nBefore a ministry instructs the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) to draft a new bill or make \nan amendment to a bill, the ministry has to seek in-principle approval from the cabinet for the \nproposed bill.  The AGC legislation division advises and helps vet or draft bills in conjunction \nwith policymakers from relevant ministries.   Public and private consultations are often \nrequested for proposed draft legislative amendments.  Thereafter, the cabinet’s approval is \nrequired before the bill can be introduced in parliament.   All bills passed by parliament (with \nsome exceptions) must be forwarded to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights for \nscrutiny, and thereafter presented to the President for assent.  Only after the President has \nassented to the bill does it become law. \nWhile ministries or regulatory agencies do conduct internal impact assessments of proposed \nreg\nulations, there are no criteria used for determining which proposed regulations are \nsubjected to an impact assessment, and there are no specific regulatory impact assessment \nguidelines. The Ministry of Finance publishes a \nbiennial Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, focusing on broad outcomes and indicators \nrather than policy evaluation.
