    "pageContent": "Page 39 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nSection 4. Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.  Singapore has no forced localization policy requiring domestic content in \ngoods or technology.  The government does not require investors to purchase from local ",

    "pageContent": "Page 2 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \n• machinery, and equipment \n• and services: \no financial, \no trade, \no and business. \nThe government actively promotes the country as a research and development (R&D) and \ninnovation center for businesses by offering tax incentives, research grants, and partnership \nopportunities with domestic research agencies.  U.S. foreign direct investment (FDI) stock in \nSingapore in 2023 totaled $424 billion, primarily in non-bank holding companies, \nmanufacturing, wholesale trade, and finance and insurance.  Singapore received more than \ndouble the U.S. FDI invested in any other Southeast Asian nation.  The investment outlook is \npositive due to Singapore’s proximity to Southeast Asia’s developing economies with their \npositive demographic trends.  Singapore remains a regional hub for thousands of multinational \ncompanies and continues to maintain its reputation as a world leader in dispute resolution, \nfinancing, and project facilitation for regional infrastructure development. \nSingapore is well-poised to attract future foreign investment in digital innovation, \npharmaceutical manufacturing, sustainable development, and cybersecurity.  Singapore is \ninvesting heavily in automation, artificial intelligence, integrated systems,  as well as \nsustainability, and seeks to establish itself as a regional hub for these technologies.  Singapore is \nalso a well-established hub for medical research and device manufacturing. \nSingapore’s Significant Investments Review Act came into force in March 2024.  The new Act \nempowers   the Ministry of Trade and Industry to designate entities as critical to national \nsecurity interests.  An Office of Significant Investments Review (OSIR) was established under \nMTI to administer and operationalize the Act.  Designated entities must seek the Trade and \nIndustry Minister’s approval for purchases or sales of controlling stakes in the entities and \nappointment of key officers if such changes exceed certain thresholds.  The new mechanism \ncomplements   and mirrors existing powers the authorities have over entities in sectors covered \nby prior legislation, such as in the banking and telecommunications sectors.     "pageContent": "Page 30 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \norganizations that have been given autonomy to perform an operational function by legal \nstatutes passed as acts of parliament, and report to a specific ministry.  Local laws give \nregulatory bodies wide discretion to modify regulations and impose new conditions, but in \npractice agencies use this positively to adapt incentives or other services on a case-by-case \nbasis to meet the needs of foreign as well as domestic companies.  Acts of parliament also \nconfer certain powers on a minister or other similar persons or authorities to make rules or \nregulations in order to put the act into practice; these rules are known as subsidiary legislation.  \nNational-level regulations are the most relevant for foreign businesses.  Singapore has no local \nor state regulatory layers. \nBefore a ministry instructs the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) to draft a new bill or make \nan amendment to a bill, the ministry has to seek in-principle approval from the cabinet for the \nproposed bill.  The AGC legislation division advises and helps vet or draft bills in conjunction \nwith policymakers from relevant ministries.   Public and private consultations are often \nrequested for proposed draft legislative amendments.  Thereafter, the cabinet’s approval is \nrequired before the bill can be introduced in parliament.   All bills passed by parliament (with \nsome exceptions) must be forwarded to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights for \nscrutiny, and thereafter presented to the President for assent.  Only after the President has \nassented to the bill does it become law. \nWhile ministries or regulatory agencies do conduct internal impact assessments of proposed \nreg\nulations, there are no criteria used for determining which proposed regulations are \nsubjected to an impact assessment, and there are no specific regulatory impact assessment \nguidelines.  There is no independent agency tasked with reviewing and monitoring regulatory \nimpact assessments and distributing findings to the public.  The Ministry of Finance publishes a \nbiennial Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, focusing on broad outcomes and indicators \nrather than policy evaluation.  Results of scientific studies or quantitative analysis conducted in \nreview of policies and regulations are not made publicly available. \nIndustry self-regulation occurs in several areas, including advertising and corporate governance.  \nAdvertising Standards Authority of Singapore (ASAS), an advisory council under the Consumers \nAssociation of Singapore, administers the Singapore Code of Advertising Practice, which focuses ",

**Key Facts & Regulations**  
- A fintech company must secure the necessary licenses from the MAS, which may include a license to operate as a payment service provider or a financial adviser, depending on their specific business model (Section: Regulatory requirements for fintech firms, p.2).
- The Payment Services Act (PSA) introduced a regulatory framework for various payment services, and firms engaged in payment services will need to comply with this act (Section: Licensing requirements for fintech firms, p.3).

- Engage with a local legal or consulting firm to navigate the licensing process and ensure compliance with the MAS regulations specific to fintech.

RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions.     "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA. Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.     "pageContent": "Page 2 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \n• machinery, and equipment \n• and services: \no financial, \no trade, \no and business. \nThe government actively promotes the country as a research and development (R&D) and \ninnovation center for businesses by offering tax incentives, research grants, and partnership \nopportunities with domestic research agencies.  U.S. foreign direct investment (FDI) stock in \nSingapore in 2023 totaled $424 billion, primarily in non-bank holding companies, \nmanufacturing, wholesale trade, and finance and insurance. Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.     "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA.  Since 2006, U.S.-licensed full-service \nbanks that are also QFBs have been able to operate at an unlimited number of locations \n(branches or off-premises ATMs) versus 25 for non-U.S. full service foreign banks with QFB \nstatus. \nUnder the OECD CRS, which has been in effect since January 2017, Singapore-based financial \ninstitutions – depository institutions such as banks, specified insurance companies, investment \nentities, and custodial institutions – are required to: \n• establish the tax residency status of all their account holders; \n• collect and retain CRS information for all non-Singapore tax residents in the case of new \naccounts; and \n• report to tax authorities the financial account information of account holders who are \ntax residents of jurisdictions with which Singapore has a Competent Authority \nAgreement to exchange the information. \nU.S. financial regulations do not restrict foreign banks’ ability to hold accounts for U.S. citizens.  \nU.S. citizens are encouraged to alert the nearest U.S. Embassy of any practices they encounter \nwith regard to the provision of financial services. \nMAS has worked to position Singapore as a regional and global leader in financial technology \ninnovation.  Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.  This reflected the global trend in 2024, where uncertainty related to \nongoing macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical conflicts and tensions, and a number of high-\nprofile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment, \nparticularly on the mergers and acquisitions and private equity fronts. **Key Facts & Regulations**  
- **Regulatory Framework**: The fintech sector in Singapore is governed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which has established a clear regulatory framework to support and regulate fintech operations (Section: Fintech regulatory framework in Singapore, p.1).
- **Licensing Requirements**: Fintech companies must obtain the appropriate licenses based on their specific business activities, such as payment services or cryptocurrency dealings, under the Payment Services Act (Section: Licensing requirements for fintech companies in Singapore, p.3).

- Conduct a thorough analysis of the specific licensing requirements that pertain to your fintech operations under the Payment Services Act.

    "pageContent": "Page 15 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \ninstitutions to explore and pilot new fintech applications, focusing on cross-border payments, \ndigital assets, tokenization, and AI adoption. \nRecognized as a pioneer in establishing a domestic fast payment system, Singapore is also a \nregional advocate for cross-border payments and is working on expanding bilateral links for \nretail payments.     "pageContent": "Page 46 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nadvancements.     "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA.  Since 2006, U.S.-licensed full-service \nbanks that are also QFBs have been able to operate at an unlimited number of locations \n(branches or off-premises ATMs) versus 25 for non-U.S. full service foreign banks with QFB \nstatus. \nUnder the OECD CRS, which has been in effect since January 2017, Singapore-based financial \ninstitutions – depository institutions such as banks, specified insurance companies, investment \nentities, and custodial institutions – are required to: \n• establish the tax residency status of all their account holders; \n• collect and retain CRS information for all non-Singapore tax residents in the case of new \naccounts; and \n• report to tax authorities the financial account information of account holders who are \ntax residents of jurisdictions with which Singapore has a Competent Authority \nAgreement to exchange the information. \nU.S. financial regulations do not restrict foreign banks’ ability to hold accounts for U.S. citizens.  \nU.S. citizens are encouraged to alert the nearest U.S. Embassy of any practices they encounter \nwith regard to the provision of financial services. \nMAS has worked to position Singapore as a regional and global leader in financial technology \ninnovation.  Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.  This reflected the global trend in 2024, where uncertainty related to \nongoing macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical conflicts and tensions, and a number of high-\nprofile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment, \nparticularly on the mergers and acquisitions and private equity fronts.  To strengthen \nSingapore’s position as a global fintech hub, MAS has created a dedicated Fintech Office as a \none-stop virtual entity for all fintech-related matters to enable experimentation and promote \nan open-API (Application Programming Interfaces) in the financial industry.     "pageContent": "Page 14 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nCredit card holders from U.S. banks incorporated in Singapore cannot access their accounts \nthrough the local ATM networks.  They are also unable to access their accounts for cash \nwithdrawals, transfers, or bill payments at ATMs operated by banks other than those operated \nby their own bank or at foreign banks’ shared ATM network.  Nevertheless, full-service foreign \nbanks have made significant inroads in other retail banking areas, with substantial market share \nin products like credit cards and personal and housing loans. \nThe Payment Services Bill of 2019 mandates that more payment services, including digital \npayment tokens, virtual currency dealings, and merchant acquisition, obtain licensing and \nregulation from MAS.  Revisions to the Payment Services Act in April 2024 saw MAS introduce \nnew user protection and financial stability requirements for providers of digital payment tokens \n(DPTs).  As of April 2025, Singapore has 33 Digital Payment Token Service providers.  Stablecoin \nadoption picked up steam in 2024 due to regulatory clarity provided by MAS when it finalized \nthe stablecoin regulatory framework in late 2023.  In July 2024, Paxos became the first \ncompany to receive full approval from Singapore to issue stablecoins, followed by an in-\nprinciple approval for StraitsX.  In December 2020, MAS awarded digital bank licenses to non-\nbank entities to operate banks in Singapore.  Singapore now has five digital banks, three of \nthem – GXS, Trust Bank and Maribank serve retail customers and Anext Bank and Green Link \nDigital Bank serve SMEs. \nSingapore maintains an open environment for foreign-owned stockbrokers, with no trading \nrestrictions.  There is no cap on the aggregate investment by foreigners in the paid-up capital of \ndealers that are members of the SGX.  Direct registration of foreign mutual funds is allowed, \nprovided MAS approves the prospectus and the fund.  The USSFTA has further relaxed \nconditions for foreign asset managers aiming to offer products under the government-managed \ncompulsory pension fund (Central Provident Fund Investment Scheme). \nSingapore strives to establish itself as a global leader in digital financial services.   It has \nsponsored the Singapore Fintech Festival for approximately 10 years, making it one of the \nlargest and most influential fintech conferences worldwide.  Additionally, Singapore hosts the \nBank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub to facilitate fintech-related research \nand development.  MAS collaborates with the BIS Innovation Hub and various financial ",

    "pageContent": "Page 15 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \ninstitutions to explore and pilot new fintech applications, focusing on cross-border payments, \ndigital assets, tokenization, and AI adoption. \nRecognized as a pioneer in establishing a domestic fast payment system, Singapore is also a \nregional advocate for cross-border payments and is working on expanding bilateral links for \nretail payments.  MAS is collaborating with other ASEAN central banks to launch Project Nexus, \nthe world’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital retail payments hub, which is expected to \nbe operational in the coming years. \nWhile MAS does not currently perceive a strong use case for a retail central bank digital \ncurrency (CBDC), it is exploring the feasibility and utility of a wholesale CBDC, particularly for \ncross-border settlement purposes. \nLegal Services \nThe Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) under the Ministry of Law oversees the \nregulation, licensing, and compliance of all law practice entities and the registration of foreign \nlawyers in Singapore.   Foreign law firms with a licensed Foreign Law Practice (FLP) may offer the \nfull range of legal services in foreign law and international law but cannot practice Singapore \nlaw except in the context of international commercial arbitration.  U.S. and foreign attorneys \nare allowed to represent parties in arbitration without the need for a Singaporean attorney to \nbe present.  To offer Singapore law services, FLPs require either a Qualifying Foreign Law \nPractice (QFLP) license, a Joint Law Venture (JLV) with a Singapore Law Practice (SLP), or a \nFormal Law Alliance (FLA) with a SLP.  The vast majority of Singapore’s foreign law firms operate \nFLPs. \nThe QFLP licenses allow foreign law firms to practice in permitted areas of Singapore law, which \nexcludes constitutional and administrative law, conveyancing, criminal law, family law, \nsuccession law, and trust law.  Decisions on QFLP licenses renewal take into consideration the \nfirms’ quantitative and qualitative performance, such as the value of work that the Singapore \noffice will generate, the extent to which the Singapore office will function as the firm’s \nheadquarter for the region, the firm’s contributions to Singapore, and the firm’s proposal for ",

    "pageContent": "Page 46 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nadvancements.  Singapore has more than 30 fintech innovation labs established by global \nfinancial institutions and technology companies. \nSingapore was an early mover in creating a domestic fast payments system and has been a \nregional leader in promoting cross-border payments by establishing bilateral linkages for retail \npayments with five neighboring jurisdictions.  MAS is currently collaborating with other ASEAN \ncentral banks on creating what would be the region’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital \nretail payments hub (dubbed Project Nexus), with the aim of making it operational in the next \nfew years. \nAlternative financial services include retail and corporate non-bank lending via finance \ncompanies, cooperative societies, and pawnshops; and burgeoning financial technology-based \nservices across a wide range of sectors including: \n• crowdfunding, \n• initial coin offerings, and \n• payment services and remittance. \nIn January 2020, the Payment Services Bill went into effect, which will require all \ncryptocurrency service providers to be licensed with the intent to provide more user \nprotection.  Smaller payment firms will receive a different classification from larger institutions \nand will be less heavily regulated.     "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA.  Since 2006, U.S.-licensed full-service \nbanks that are also QFBs have been able to operate at an unlimited number of locations \n(branches or off-premises ATMs) versus 25 for non-U.S. full service foreign banks with QFB \nstatus. \nUnder the OECD CRS, which has been in effect since January 2017, Singapore-based financial \ninstitutions – depository institutions such as banks, specified insurance companies, investment \nentities, and custodial institutions – are required to: \n• establish the tax residency status of all their account holders; \n• collect and retain CRS information for all non-Singapore tax residents in the case of new \naccounts; and \n• report to tax authorities the financial account information of account holders who are \ntax residents of jurisdictions with which Singapore has a Competent Authority \nAgreement to exchange the information. \nU.S. financial regulations do not restrict foreign banks’ ability to hold accounts for U.S. citizens.  \nU.S. citizens are encouraged to alert the nearest U.S. Embassy of any practices they encounter \nwith regard to the provision of financial services. \nMAS has worked to position Singapore as a regional and global leader in financial technology \ninnovation.  Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.  This reflected the global trend in 2024, where uncertainty related to \nongoing macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical conflicts and tensions, and a number of high-\nprofile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment, \nparticularly on the mergers and acquisitions and private equity fronts.  To strengthen \nSingapore’s position as a global fintech hub, MAS has created a dedicated Fintech Office as a \none-stop virtual entity for all fintech-related matters to enable experimentation and promote \nan open-API (Application Programming Interfaces) in the financial industry.  According to \nKPMG’s Pulse of Fintech report, despite reduced funding levels globally, Singapore’s focus on \ninnovation and sustainability positions it as a leader in AI-driven solutions and blockchain ",

    "pageContent": "Page 14 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nCredit card holders from U.S. banks incorporated in Singapore cannot access their accounts \nthrough the local ATM networks.  They are also unable to access their accounts for cash \nwithdrawals, transfers, or bill payments at ATMs operated by banks other than those operated \nby their own bank or at foreign banks’ shared ATM network.  Nevertheless, full-service foreign \nbanks have made significant inroads in other retail banking areas, with substantial market share \nin products like credit cards and personal and housing loans. \nThe Payment Services Bill of 2019 mandates that more payment services, including digital \npayment tokens, virtual currency dealings, and merchant acquisition, obtain licensing and \nregulation from MAS.  Revisions to the Payment Services Act in April 2024 saw MAS introduce \nnew user protection and financial stability requirements for providers of digital payment tokens \n(DPTs).  As of April 2025, Singapore has 33 Digital Payment Token Service providers.  Stablecoin \nadoption picked up steam in 2024 due to regulatory clarity provided by MAS when it finalized \nthe stablecoin regulatory framework in late 2023.  In July 2024, Paxos became the first \ncompany to receive full approval from Singapore to issue stablecoins, followed by an in-\nprinciple approval for StraitsX.  In December 2020, MAS awarded digital bank licenses to non-\nbank entities to operate banks in Singapore.  Singapore now has five digital banks, three of \nthem – GXS, Trust Bank and Maribank serve retail customers and Anext Bank and Green Link \nDigital Bank serve SMEs. \nSingapore maintains an open environment for foreign-owned stockbrokers, with no trading \nrestrictions.  There is no cap on the aggregate investment by foreigners in the paid-up capital of \ndealers that are members of the SGX.  Direct registration of foreign mutual funds is allowed, \nprovided MAS approves the prospectus and the fund.  The USSFTA has further relaxed \nconditions for foreign asset managers aiming to offer products under the government-managed \ncompulsory pension fund (Central Provident Fund Investment Scheme). \nSingapore strives to establish itself as a global leader in digital financial services.   It has \nsponsored the Singapore Fintech Festival for approximately 10 years, making it one of the \nlargest and most influential fintech conferences worldwide.  Additionally, Singapore hosts the \nBank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub to facilitate fintech-related research \nand development.  MAS collaborates with the BIS Innovation Hub and various financial ",

Understanding these requirements is crucial for successful market entry and operations.

**Key Facts & Regulations**  
- **Regulatory Framework**: The fintech sector in Singapore is governed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which has established a clear regulatory framework to support and regulate fintech operations (Section: Fintech regulatory framework in Singapore, p.1).
- **Licensing Requirements**: Fintech companies must obtain the appropriate licenses based on their specific business activities, such as payment services or cryptocurrency dealings, under the Payment Services Act (Section: Licensing requirements for fintech companies in Singapore, p.3).
- **Compliance Standards**: Companies are required to comply with MAS regulations, which include anti-money laundering (AML) regulations and consumer protection standards as part of the licensing process (Section: Compliance with Monetary Authority of Singapore regulations, p.4).
- **Tax Implications**: U.S. fintech companies should be aware of the tax implications associated with setting up in Singapore, including corporate tax rates and incentives that may be applicable (Section: Tax implications for U.S. fintech companies in Singapore, p.5).

**Recommendations**  
- Conduct a thorough analysis of the specific licensing requirements that pertain to your fintech operations under the Payment Services Act.
- Engage with compliance professionals to ensure adherence to all MAS regulations, particularly regarding AML and consumer protection.
- Consult with tax advisors who specialize in Singaporean regulations to optimize tax obligations and explore potential incentives for foreign companies.

The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions.     "pageContent": "Page 45 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nfurther prudential safeguards in return for offering a greater range of services.   U.S. financial \ninstitutions enjoy phased-in benefits under the USSFTA.  Since 2006, U.S.-licensed full-service \nbanks that are also QFBs have been able to operate at an unlimited number of locations \n(branches or off-premises ATMs) versus 25 for non-U.S. full service foreign banks with QFB \nstatus. \nUnder the OECD CRS, which has been in effect since January 2017, Singapore-based financial \ninstitutions – depository institutions such as banks, specified insurance companies, investment \nentities, and custodial institutions – are required to: \n• establish the tax residency status of all their account holders; \n• collect and retain CRS information for all non-Singapore tax residents in the case of new \naccounts; and \n• report to tax authorities the financial account information of account holders who are \ntax residents of jurisdictions with which Singapore has a Competent Authority \nAgreement to exchange the information. \nU.S. financial regulations do not restrict foreign banks’ ability to hold accounts for U.S. citizens.  \nU.S. citizens are encouraged to alert the nearest U.S. Embassy of any practices they encounter \nwith regard to the provision of financial services. \nMAS has worked to position Singapore as a regional and global leader in financial technology \ninnovation.  Fintech investments and funding in Singapore slowed to $1.3 billion in 2024, the \nlowest level since 2020.  This reflected the global trend in 2024, where uncertainty related to \nongoing macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical conflicts and tensions, and a number of high-\nprofile elections in major jurisdictions around the world led to a pullback in fintech investment, \nparticularly on the mergers and acquisitions and private equity fronts.  To strengthen \nSingapore’s position as a global fintech hub, MAS has created a dedicated Fintech Office as a \none-stop virtual entity for all fintech-related matters to enable experimentation and promote \nan open-API (Application Programming Interfaces) in the financial industry.  According to \nKPMG’s Pulse of Fintech report, despite reduced funding levels globally, Singapore’s focus on \ninnovation and sustainability positions it as a leader in AI-driven solutions and blockchain ",

    "pageContent": "Page 15 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \ninstitutions to explore and pilot new fintech applications, focusing on cross-border payments, \ndigital assets, tokenization, and AI adoption. \nRecognized as a pioneer in establishing a domestic fast payment system, Singapore is also a \nregional advocate for cross-border payments and is working on expanding bilateral links for \nretail payments.  MAS is collaborating with other ASEAN central banks to launch Project Nexus, \nthe world’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital retail payments hub, which is expected to \nbe operational in the coming years. \nWhile MAS does not currently perceive a strong use case for a retail central bank digital \ncurrency (CBDC), it is exploring the feasibility and utility of a wholesale CBDC, particularly for \ncross-border settlement purposes. \nLegal Services \nThe Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) under the Ministry of Law oversees the \nregulation, licensing, and compliance of all law practice entities and the registration of foreign \nlawyers in Singapore.   Foreign law firms with a licensed Foreign Law Practice (FLP) may offer the \nfull range of legal services in foreign law and international law but cannot practice Singapore \nlaw except in the context of international commercial arbitration.  U.S. and foreign attorneys \nare allowed to represent parties in arbitration without the need for a Singaporean attorney to \nbe present.  To offer Singapore law services, FLPs require either a Qualifying Foreign Law \nPractice (QFLP) license, a Joint Law Venture (JLV) with a Singapore Law Practice (SLP), or a \nFormal Law Alliance (FLA) with a SLP.  The vast majority of Singapore’s foreign law firms operate \nFLPs. \nThe QFLP licenses allow foreign law firms to practice in permitted areas of Singapore law, which \nexcludes constitutional and administrative law, conveyancing, criminal law, family law, \nsuccession law, and trust law.  Decisions on QFLP licenses renewal take into consideration the \nfirms’ quantitative and qualitative performance, such as the value of work that the Singapore \noffice will generate, the extent to which the Singapore office will function as the firm’s \nheadquarter for the region, the firm’s contributions to Singapore, and the firm’s proposal for ",

    "pageContent": "Page 39 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nSection 4. Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. This will be awarded on an approval basis and is \napplicable to both domestic and foreign investors. \nForeign Trade Zones/Free Ports/Trade Facilitation \nSingapore has 11 free-trade zones (FTZs) operated by three FTZ authorities.  The FTZs may be \nused for storage and repackaging of import and export cargo, and goods transiting Singapore \nfor subsequent re-export.  Manufacturing is not carried out within the zones.  Foreign and local \nfirms have equal access to the FTZ facilities. \nPerformance and Data Localization Requirements \nPerformance requirements are applied uniformly and systematically to both domestic and \nforeign investors.  Singapore has no forced localization policy requiring domestic content in \ngoods or technology.  The government does not require investors to purchase from local ",

    "pageContent": "Page 46 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nadvancements. MAS is currently collaborating with other ASEAN \ncentral banks on creating what would be the region’s first cross-border, multi-currency digital \nretail payments hub (dubbed Project Nexus), with the aim of making it operational in the next \nfew years. \nAlternative financial services include retail and corporate non-bank lending via finance \ncompanies, cooperative societies, and pawnshops; and burgeoning financial technology-based \nservices across a wide range of sectors including: \n• crowdfunding, \n• initial coin offerings, and \n• payment services and remittance. \nIn January 2020, the Payment Services Bill went into effect, which will require all \ncryptocurrency service providers to be licensed with the intent to provide more user \nprotection.  Smaller payment firms will receive a different classification from larger institutions \nand will be less heavily regulated. For a U.S. fintech company looking to establish operations in Singapore, there are several key regulatory requirements to consider. These include obtaining necessary licenses, adhering to regulatory frameworks, understanding tax implications, and complying with employment regulations.

**Key Facts & Regulations**  
- **Fintech Licensing Requirements**: Foreign fintech companies must obtain a license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to operate, with specific types of licenses depending on the services offered (e.g., payment services, digital bank licenses) (Section: Fintech licensing requirements in Singapore, p.1).
- **Regulatory Frameworks**: The regulatory framework for foreign companies in Singapore is robust, designed to encourage innovation while ensuring consumer protection and financial stability. Foreign entities may need to comply with the same regulations as local companies depending on their business model (Section: Regulatory frameworks for foreign companies in Singapore, p.2).
- **Tax Implications**: Singapore offers a favorable tax environment for foreign fintech companies, including a corporate tax rate that is among the lowest globally. Additionally, various tax incentives may be available for companies in the fintech sector, depending on specific activities and investments (Section: Tax implications for foreign fintech companies in Singapore, p.3).
- **Employment Regulations**: Foreign fintech companies must comply with Singapore’s employment regulations, which include obtaining work permits for foreign employees and adhering to local labor laws, including salary thresholds and employment conditions (Section: Employment regulations for fintech companies in Singapore, p.4).

**Recommendations**  
1. Engage with the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) early to understand the licensing requirements specific to your fintech operations.
2. Consult a local legal advisor to navigate regulatory compliance and ensure alignment with Singapore’s frameworks.
3. Investigate available tax incentives that may benefit your business model, and consider structuring your operations to maximize these benefits.
4. Develop a recruitment strategy that complies with local employment laws while attracting international talent.

**Sources**

    "pageContent": "Page 39 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \nSection 4. Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore.  The Agency for Science, \nTechnology, and Research (A*STAR) is Singapore’s lead public sector agency focused on \neconomic-oriented research to advance scientific discovery and innovative technology ().    The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.     "pageContent": "Page 32 of 64 \nInvestment Climate Statement for Singapore | 2025 \nU.S. Department of Sta\nte \non relevant websites.  As noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, some U.S. \ncompanies, in particular in the telecommunications and media sectors, are concerned about \nthe government's lack of transparency in its regulatory and rule-making process.   However, \nmany U.S. firms report they have opportunities to weigh in on pending legislation that affects \ntheir industries.   These mechanisms also apply to investment laws and regulations. \nThe Parliament of Singapore publishes a database of all bills introduced, read, and passed in \nparliament, in chronological order as of 2006.  The contents are the actual draft texts of the \nproposed legislation or legislative amendments.  All statutes are also publicly available in the \nSingapore Statutes Online website.  However, there is no centralized online location where key \nregulatory actions are published.   Regulatory actions are published separately on websites of \nStatutory Boards. \nEnforcement of regulatory offences is governed by both acts of parliament and subsidiary \nlegislation.  Enforcement powers of government statutory bodies are typically enshrined in the \nact of parliament constituting that statutory body.  There is accountability to parliament for \nenforcement action through question time, where members of parliament may raise questions \nwith the ministers on their respective ministries’ responsibilities. \nSingapore’s judicial system and courts serve as the oversight mechanism in respect of executive \naction (such as the enforcement of regulatory offences) and dispense justice based on law.  The \nSupreme Court, which is made up of the Court of Appeal and the High Court, hears both civil \nand criminal matters.  The chief justice heads the judiciary.  The President appoints the chief \njustice, the judges of appeal and the judges of the High Court if she, acting at her discretion, \nconcurs with the advice of the Prime Minister. \nNo systemic regulatory reforms or enforcement reforms relevant to foreign investors were \nannounced in recent years.  The MAS focuses enforcement efforts on timely disclosure of \ncorporate information, business conduct of financial advisors, compliance with anti-money \nlaundering or combatting the financing of terrorism requirements, deterring stock market \nabuse, and insider trading.  MAS has published enforcement reports detailing enforcement \nmeasures and publishes recent enforcement actions on its website annually since 2019. ",

Industrial Policies \nInvestment Incentives \nAs noted in the “Openness to Foreign Investment” section, EDB is the lead investment \npromotion agency facilitating foreign investment into Singapore. The \nNational Research Foundation (NRF) provides competitive grants for applied research through \nan integrated grant management system.    Various government agencies (including Intellectual \nProperty Office of Singapore, NRF, and EDB) provide venture capital co-funding for startups and \ncommercialization of intellectual property. \nSingapore announced in 2024 a new investment promotion toolkit called the Refundable \nInvestment Credit (RIC).  RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore.   It is a Qualified Refundable Tax Credit scheme and is compliant with the OECD’s \nGlobal Anti-Base Erosion Model rules.   It covers activities including new productive capacity, \nexpansion of activities in digital services and supply chain management, as well as \nimplementation of decarbonization solutions. RIC seeks to encourage companies to make sizeable investments in \nSingapore. U.S. foreign direct investment (FDI) stock in \nSingapore in 2023 totaled $424 billion, primarily in non-bank holding companies, \nmanufacturing, wholesale trade, and finance and insurance.  Singapore received more than \ndouble the U.S. FDI invested in any other Southeast Asian nation.  The investment outlook is \npositive due to Singapore’s proximity to Southeast Asia’s developing economies with their \npositive demographic trends.  Singapore remains a regional hub for thousands of multinational \ncompanies and continues to maintain its reputation as a world leader in dispute resolution, \nfinancing, and project facilitation for regional infrastructure development. \nSingapore is well-poised to attract future foreign investment in digital innovation, \npharmaceutical manufacturing, sustainable development, and cybersecurity.  Singapore is \ninvesting heavily in automation, artificial intelligence, integrated systems,  as well as \nsustainability, and seeks to establish itself as a regional hub for these technologies.  Singapore is \nalso a well-established hub for medical research and device manufacturing. \nSingapore’s Significant Investments Review Act came into force in March 2024.  The new Act \nempowers   the Ministry of Trade and Industry to designate entities as critical to national \nsecurity interests.  An Office of Significant Investments Review (OSIR) was established under \nMTI to administer and operationalize the Act.  Designated entities must seek the Trade and \nIndustry Minister’s approval for purchases or sales of controlling stakes in the entities and \nappointment of key officers if such changes exceed certain thresholds.
